A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SelfMOTR work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and v2 Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original SelfMOTR experiments on DanceTrack and MOT17, detection-prior ablations, detection–association analyses, and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds BFT and AnimalTrack results, decoder-attention measurements, and a shorter-clip MOT17 experiment.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same shared-parameter detection and tracking passes, confidence-conditioned proposal queries, ten additional learned anchors, and proposal-loss weight of 0.5. The added distillation equation explains an existing strategy, and the attention diagnostics do not alter the tracking algorithm. Denoising was already present in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual training and evaluation on BFT and AnimalTrack, extending human tracking to birds and other animals with deformation, occlusion, and different motion conditions. DanceTrack, MOT17, and the existing COCO/CrowdHuman training resources remain represented; MOT17 moves to Appendix A.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 introduces reported comparisons with JDE, FairMOT, CenterTrack, SORT, QDTrack, TransCenter, and TransTrack, beyond the comparator set evaluated in v1. Conversely, the MOT17 comparison drops SUSHI, CoNo-Link, ByteTrack, GHOST, and OC-SORT. DanceTrack comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds 20-epoch BFT and AnimalTrack training protocols, learning-rate decay at epoch 16, and respective re-identification windows of 15 and 10. Appendix A adds a three-frame MOT17 training condition alongside the original five-frame condition. Section 4.4 and Appendix B introduce layer-wise and token-level attention evaluation. The existing DanceTrack training schedule and tracking metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine whether detect queries disproportionately attend to existing tracks, comparing attention mass and entropy across decoder layers and between MOTR and SelfMOTR. Appendix B extends these diagnostics across three datasets, and Appendix A tests MOT17 clip length. Earlier component, proposal-source, threshold, data-scaling, and decoder-depth ablations are retained, sometimes relocated or consolidated.

E5.justification: v2 newly presents KDE estimates of token-level attention distributions in Figures 5b and 7, plus shaded bands around layer-wise averages in Figure 5a. The bands' statistical meaning is unspecified. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, defined confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds BFT and AnimalTrack results, including SelfMOTR HOTA of 71.1 and 45.5, and new attention-distribution findings. MOT17's original 57.5 HOTA is retained alongside 58.4 under the new three-frame condition, rather than a same-setting improvement. DanceTrack SelfMOTR remains at 69.2 HOTA, while MeMOTR's reported HOTA changes from 63.4 to 68.5. SPAM's MOT17 MOTA changes from 89.2 to 80.7.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.4 introduces a mathematical definition of cardinality-corrected Track-Attention Mass and defines normalized attention entropy for the new diagnostic analysis. This is a limited formal addition; the SelfMOTR equations remain equivalent, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add attention imbalance as a central diagnostic contribution and a leading-performance claim on BFT. The introduction and conclusion also advocate internal prior generation as a default design principle for unified tracking. This substantially broadens v1's contribution framing around MOTR's hidden detector, prior-injection strategies, and competitive DanceTrack performance.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations linking attention polarization to impaired discovery and linking dataset-dependent attention to target deformation. Appendix A explains that shorter MOT17 clips improve detection while slightly harming association and do not close the competitive gap. Conversely, v1's explicit limitation that integration into CO-MOT or MOTRv3 remains untested is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link, animal-dataset training settings, and explicit attribution of the existing query-denoising strategy. It omits v1's MOT17-specific 180-epoch training budget and learning-rate decay every 80 epochs. Most optimizer, preprocessing, initialization, and runtime-hardware details are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds attention-sink studies as conceptual inspiration, together with references for new datasets, comparators, and denoising. The MOTChallenge reference is removed. The central positioning against external-detector MOTRv2/MOTRv3 and CO-MOT's additional query management remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work narrative, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Related work gains thematic subheadings, the explicit contribution list and standalone Discussion section disappear, and MOT17 plus selected ablations move into new appendices. These changes substantially reorganize the paper's narrative.

P2.justification: v2 changes from a two-column to a single-column layout, redraws the SelfMOTR architecture diagram, adds attention plots and the animal-benchmark table, and consolidates several ablation tables. It also corrects Figure 2's reversed track-query legend labels. Figures and tables are extensively resized and relocated; generic running-header placeholders remain in v2.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the unchanged method: Table 3 tests applicability in two non-human domains absent from v1, while Section 4.4 and Appendix B provide measurements directly relevant to query interference. Figure 2 also resolves contradictory condition labels. These gains outweigh the omitted MOT17 training-budget details, although the attention evidence remains correlational and the target-trained animal experiments do not establish the claimed transfer beyond the training regime.
